name: Placenta capsules

card.summary: Dehydrated, encapsulated placenta taken after birth, promoted by proponents for postpartum energy, mood and recovery.
card.note: The CDC reported a newborn infection linked to a mother taking placenta capsules.

quick.overview:
Placenta capsules are made by steaming and drying a mother's placenta and putting the powder into capsules, which she takes after giving birth. Services offer the preparation at home, and it is the most common form of human placentophagy.

Proponents say it improves energy, mood, lactation and postpartum recovery, which they associate with feeling and looking more rested. Randomized pilot trials have measured mood, hormones, iron and prolactin, and reviews report no demonstrated clinical benefit.
quick.how: The mother's placenta is typically prepared by a specialist, steamed and dehydrated, ground and placed in capsules that are taken in the weeks after birth. Other forms include smoothies, tinctures and raw or cooked placenta.
quick.risks: The CDC described a 2017 case of late-onset group B Streptococcus infection in a newborn probably linked to the mother's placenta capsules and advised against the practice. A 2018 review recommended physicians discourage it, and obstetric bodies in Canada and elsewhere have issued statements on it.

lead: Placenta capsules are dried, powdered human placenta taken orally after childbirth. The placenta is usually steamed and dehydrated, then encapsulated; it can also be eaten raw, cooked, or in smoothies and tinctures [1]. Human placentophagy is a recent trend among some women in affluent countries, and few human cultures have customarily eaten placenta [1][2].

Advocates say it helps mood, energy and lactation and speeds postpartum recovery; in a survey by anthropologists, about three-quarters of respondents who ate their placenta reported benefits such as improved mood, energy and lactation [2]. The link to looks is an indirect one: practitioners present it as supporting recovery, rest and wellbeing after birth.

Research is limited to pilot trials and reviews. A 2018 review found no scientific evidence of clinical benefit and reported that placental nutrients and hormones are not retained in useful amounts after encapsulation [1]. The CDC reported a newborn infection in 2017 and advised avoiding capsules [2].

chain: Proponents say it aids energy, mood and postpartum recovery
Claimed: better rest and recovery, a fresher postpartum appearance
angle.text: Proponents take placenta capsules in the postpartum period to support energy, mood and recovery. Trials have measured mood, hormones and iron, but not appearance.

paras: Encapsulation after steaming and dehydration is the most frequent preparation, offered by numerous companies [1]. Traditional Chinese medicine has used dried human placenta (ziheche) for wasting diseases, infertility and impotence, but there is little evidence that eating placenta was customary in other cultures [2]. In 1998 BBC reported that Channel 4 criticised chef Hugh Fearnley-Whittingstall for cooking and eating a human placenta on television [2].

Advocates claim it prevents postpartum depression, reduces fatigue, improves bonding and raises milk supply [3][4]. Animal studies, mainly in rats, suggest placenta and amniotic fluid can enhance opioid-mediated pain relief through a placental opioid-enhancing factor; this has not been tested in humans [3][5].

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot of 27 mothers compared encapsulated placenta with placebo for mood, bonding and fatigue [4]. A companion pilot examined maternal salivary hormones [6]. A randomized pilot found placenta capsules did not change postpartum plasma prolactin or newborn weight gain [7], and another examined maternal iron status [8]. A 2018 review concluded there is no scientific evidence of clinical benefit and that hormones and nutrients are not retained in useful amounts [1]. A lab analysis found encapsulated placenta contains modest concentrations of 14 trace minerals [9]. The Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada issued a placentophagy guideline [10].

The CDC reported a newborn with late-onset group B Streptococcus infection likely caused by the mother's placenta capsules and advised avoiding them [2]. A 2018 review concluded the practice is potentially harmful with no documented benefit and that doctors should discourage it [2]. A Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists spokesperson said there is no medical reason to eat the placenta when well nourished [2].

timeline.event: Chef eats placenta on British TV, drawing criticism.[2]
CDC reports infant GBS infection linked to placenta capsules.[2]
Review advises physicians to discourage the practice.[1][2]
